target_customer: Individuals and small teams who need to send very large files, with a paid tier for people who need end-to-end encryption
problem: Email and cloud storage services limit or charge for large file transfers, and cloud links expose files to the provider. WireOver offered free unlimited peer-to-peer sending with an optional encrypted mode.
business_model: Freemium desktop app; free unlimited unencrypted transfers, Pro plan at about 10 dollars a month for end-to-end encrypted transfers

founders.name: Amit Bansil
founders.background_notes: YC page: Boston programmer who began in the late 1990s writing interactive chemistry simulation tools, later built truck dispatching software and software for preventing adolescent substance abuse. Education not listed.

founders.name: Trenton Ashburn
prior_employers: Quantitative hedge funds (computational models, firms unnamed)
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch 2014 calls him Trent Ashburn and says he built computational models for quantitative hedge funds and was a semi-pro cyclist. YC page lists him as founder with no bio.

competitors.name: YouSendIt
competitors.what: Paid and free service for sending files too large for email, expanding into cloud storage
competitors.traction_then: Established large-file sending service; positioned against Dropbox in a January 2008 CMSWire piece

technical_complexity.rationale: A Python desktop client with peer-to-peer transfer plus relay fallback and optional end-to-end encryption with fingerprint verification, built by two people. NAT traversal and both-sides-online coordination were the hard parts.

defensibility.rationale: File transfer was a crowded category with free alternatives, and the product required both parties online, which limited stickiness. Encryption was a feature others could copy.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: TechCrunch in January 2014 framed Dropbox, Google Drive and SkyDrive as the incumbents WireOver wanted to beat on security. No acquisition or copycat is documented in sources found.

market_need_then: Free tools capped file sizes and cloud services charged for storage; the 2014 TechCrunch piece tied demand for private transfer to mass surveillance news.

branding.domain_note: Operated at wireover.com; no source on how the domain was obtained

identity.voice_and_tone: Security-first positioning with a Trust No One message (TechCrunch 2014)

branding.community_and_virality: A Show HN post in March 2012 and blog coverage by TechPP the same month; TechCrunch coverage in January 2014

brand_strength.rationale: Some tech press coverage and a Show HN post, but no evidence of a distinctive brand asset or community.

outcome_analysis: The cause of WireOver's inactivity is not public: no shutdown post or post-mortem was found. The product emerged from stealth with Bessemer and .406 Ventures backing in January 2014, yet the YC directory lists it as inactive and its site returned errors. The failure factors chosen are inferences from a crowded category of free large-file tools with the requirement that both parties be online, not stated causes.
notes: Cause of inactivity not public; no shutdown date found. The 120000 dollar seed rests on a single aggregator (Kando) as reported in a search summary; the page itself could not be fetched. The second round has Bessemer, .406 Ventures and angel Hayes Metzger per TechCrunch but no amount or date. wireover.com returned HTTP 503. Failure factors are low-confidence inferences.
